title: TLS Certificate Validation
source_note: Inspired by Apple's famous 'goto fail' TLS bug.
summary: Review this certificate-validation helper and find the single line that fatally changes the control flow.
explanation: The unconditional 'goto fail;' exits the verification path even when hashing succeeded, so the later signature verification never meaningfully protects the handshake.
hints: The flaw is in the verification flow, not the setup code.
One line exits early even when the previous operation succeeded.
Look for a control-flow statement that skips the final cryptographic check.
The unconditional jump on line 31 is the problem.

title: Community Vault Withdrawal
source_note: Inspired by The DAO reentrancy bug family.

explanation: The contract sends value to the caller before updating their stored balance. A malicious receiver can re-enter withdraw while the old balance is still intact.
hints: The bug depends on the order of side effects.
State is updated too late relative to an external interaction.
Find the line that hands control to attacker-controlled code before the balance changes.
The external call on line 22 should not happen before the balance update.

title: Warehouse Robot Dispatch Window
source_note: Original puzzle about a dispatch gate for scheduled warehouse robot runs.
summary: This launch helper checks battery level and the scheduled time window before dispatching a robot. One boolean expression weakens the final readiness gate.
code: export function canDispatchRobot(window: DispatchWindow, currentMinute: number): boolean {
explanation: Dispatch should require both the robot to be ready and the launch slot to be reserved. Line 23 uses `||`, so a robot can launch with only one of those required conditions satisfied.
hints: The battery and time-window checks are fine.
The flaw is in how the final go/no-go condition is combined.
Look for a boolean expression that accepts either prerequisite when the scheduler really needs both.
The `window.ready || window.slotReserved` expression on line 23 is the flaw.

title: Motor Schedule Frame Decoder
source_note: Original puzzle about decoding a compact motor-controller schedule frame.
summary: This decoder reads a count-prefixed schedule frame into a fixed-size structure. One loop trusts the incoming count too much.
code: int decode_motor_schedule(const uint8_t *frame, size_t frame_length, MotorSchedule *out_schedule) {
explanation: The frame length check proves the packet contains enough bytes, but line 32 never verifies that `slot_count` fits inside the fixed `slots` array. A malicious frame can set `slot_count` above 12 and overflow `out_schedule->slots`.
hints: The packet-length arithmetic is not the main issue.
The destination structure has a fixed maximum capacity.
Look for the line that iterates based only on untrusted input without first capping it to `MAX_SCHEDULE_SLOTS`.
The `for` loop on line 32 is the flaw.

title: Embedded Telemetry Poller
source_note: Original puzzle about a sampler goroutine for embedded telemetry collection.
summary: This helper starts a ticker using a millisecond configuration value. One line converts the interval using the wrong unit.
code: func StartTelemetrySampler(cfg SamplerConfig, readSensor func(string) error) *time.Ticker {
explanation: `PollIntervalMs` is documented in milliseconds, but line 21 multiplies it by `time.Second`. A configured value like 500 becomes 500 seconds instead of half a second.
hints: The fallback value and goroutine loop are both reasonable.
The bug is in the translation from config units to a `time.Duration`.
Look for the line that treats millisecond input as if it were in a larger unit.
The ticker creation on line 21 is the flaw.

title: Firmware Rollout Queue Permission
source_note: Original puzzle about approving scheduled firmware rollouts for field devices.
summary: This permission helper checks admins, named approvers, and team leads before allowing a rollout to be queued. One shortcut confuses timing metadata with authorization.
explanation: A maintenance window describes when a rollout may occur, not who is allowed to queue it. Line 22 grants permission to any authenticated user whenever the window is open.
hints: The admin and explicit-approver checks are fine.
The flaw mixes scheduling state with an access-control decision.
Look for a `return True` that depends on rollout timing rather than the caller's role or identity.
The `return True` on line 22 is the flaw.

title: Charging Port Reservation
source_note: Original puzzle about scheduling a charging window on a multi-port dock.
summary: This function reserves a dock port, programs the charging window, and enables power. One required operation reports success or failure, but the result is ignored.
code: fun programWindow(portId: String, startMinute: Int, durationMinutes: Int): Boolean
fun scheduleChargeJob(job: ChargeJob, bus: ChargerBus, audit: AuditLog): Boolean {
explanation: Line 28 ignores whether `reservePort` succeeded. The function may continue to program and enable a port that was never actually reserved for this job.
hints: The `programWindow` and `enablePort` calls are both checked.
One earlier bus operation can fail, but the function proceeds as if it always worked.
Look for the API call whose Boolean result is discarded before the rest of the schedule is applied.
The `bus.reservePort(job.portId)` call on line 28 is the flaw.

title: Brake Table Uploader
source_note: Original puzzle about uploading a braking profile to an embedded motion controller.
summary: This uploader opens a device, writes a header, waits for an acknowledgement, and then streams table rows. One failure path skips cleanup after the device is already open.
code: bool uploadBrakeTable(const std::string& devicePath, const BrakeTable& table) {
explanation: If the acknowledgement never arrives, line 23 returns without closing the already-open device handle. That leaks the file resource on the timeout path.
hints: The success path closes the device correctly.
The problem happens after `port` has already been opened and used.
Look for an early return in the middle of the function that skips `std::fclose(port)`.
The `return false;` on line 23 is the flaw.

title: Robot Arm Heartbeat Service
source_note: Original puzzle about a service that periodically publishes robot-arm health snapshots.
summary: This service starts a periodic heartbeat and loads the initial arm snapshot from storage. One line starts the periodic work before the data it needs is initialized.
code: public ArmHeartbeatService(ScheduledExecutorService executor, StatusBus statusBus, ArmStateCache stateCache) {
explanation: Line 17 starts the scheduled publisher before `latestSnapshot` is loaded. The first tick can run immediately and publish a null or uninitialized snapshot.
hints: The constructor wiring is straightforward.
The bug is about what happens first when `start()` is called.
Look for a line that can trigger `publishSnapshot()` before the snapshot field has been populated.
The `scheduleAtFixedRate(...)` call on line 17 is the flaw.

title: Charging Job Launcher
source_note: Original puzzle about advancing queued charging jobs into a running state.
summary: This function loads a job, marks it running in the store, and updates local fields before saving. One final write uses stale state and can undo a newer store update.
code: fn mark_running(&self, job_id: &str, started_minute: u32) -> Result<(), RepoError>;
fn save(&self, job: ChargeJob) -> Result<(), RepoError>;
pub fn launch_due_job(job_id: &str, repo: &dyn JobRepo, current_minute: u32) -> Result<bool, RepoError> {
explanation: `mark_running` updates the stored job state, but line 30 immediately saves the older in-memory `job`, which still has `state == "queued"`. That stale write can overwrite the newer running state in the repository.
hints: The early `return Ok(false)` checks are fine.
The problem appears after the repository has already been updated once.
Look for a later write that persists an older snapshot of the job after `mark_running` changes the authoritative state.
The `repo.save(job)?;` line on line 30 is the flaw.

title: Irrigation Slot Copier
source_note: Original puzzle about copying daily watering slots into a controller schedule.
summary: This helper copies validated watering slots into the controller's fixed-size day schedule. One loop runs one step too far.
code: int copy_day_schedule(const WaterSlot *input_slots, size_t slot_count, DaySchedule *out_schedule) {
explanation: When `slot_count` is the number of valid entries, the last valid index is `slot_count - 1`. Line 23 uses `<=`, so it copies one extra element and writes past the intended range.
hints: The null and maximum-count checks are fine.
The bug is in the boundary of the copy loop itself.
Look for a loop condition that includes one index beyond the last valid slot.
The `index <= slot_count` condition on line 24 is the flaw.

title: IMU Calibration Gate
source_note: Original puzzle about checking whether a sensor package is calibrated before sampling begins.
summary: This helper loads a calibration profile and verifies that it is approved for the expected axis count. One line assumes the profile lookup can never fail.
code: public boolean canStartSampling(String deviceId, int expectedAxisCount) {
explanation: `calibrationStore.load(deviceId)` can plausibly return `null` when a device has never been calibrated. Line 15 dereferences `profile` without checking for that case.
hints: The axis-count comparison is not the problem.
The risky assumption happens right after the profile is loaded.
Look for a method call on an object that may not exist for an uncalibrated device.
The `profile.isApproved()` call on line 15 is the flaw.
